1:
Gill fills in what "after these things" points back to: the battle of the kings, the captivity of Lot, the rescue of him and of the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the conversation that passed between Abram and the kings of Sodom and Salem. Henry makes both events reasons for the visit. It came after that famous act of generous charity in rescuing his neighbours out of distress, and that not for price nor reward — those that show favour to men shall find favour with God; and it came after the victory over four kings, lest Abram should be too much elevated with it, God coming to tell him that he had better things in store. Calvin asks why the vision was needed at all, since Abram's affairs were prosperous and the Lord here speaks to him as one sorrowful and afflicted with fear. Some conjecture an annoyance Moses does not mention; Calvin thinks the cause different. Though applauded on all sides, Abram had so provoked Chedorlaomer and his allies that they might attack again with fresh troops; and since signal success commonly draws envy along with it, he was now formidable and an object of suspicion to many, some fearing he would turn against his neighbours the strength he had tried against foreign kings.

On the manner of the revelation the witnesses divide. Keil and Delitzsch call this a new revelation differing from the previous ones in form and substance, and a new turning point in Abram's life: the word of Jehovah came to him in a vision, that is, neither by a direct internal address, nor by such a manifestation of himself as fell upon the outward senses, nor in a dream of the night, but in a state of ecstasy by an inward spiritual intuition, and that in the day-time. The expression applies to the whole chapter, they hold, since there is no pause anywhere, so that the whole process is to be regarded as internal. Ellicott dates it otherwise — the revelation on this occasion is made by night, though not in a dream but in a trance, in which the senses of Abram were closed to all earthly impressions and he became passive in the hands of the Almighty. He adds that the phrase, used so constantly afterwards to signify revelation, occurs here for the first time. Clarke notes the same, observing that some learned men take the Hebrew for the word of the Lord in the sense of the Logos, the Chaldee paraphrases rendering it "my word" and appearing always to consider it a person, distinct from a word merely spoken.

Calvin puts the promise before the exhortation. Though it comes last in the text it has precedence in order, since the security God urges has no foundation unless by faith we understand that he cares for us; so the causal particle belongs there — fear not, Abram, because I am thy shield. By the word shield he signifies that Abram would always be safe under his protection, and we ought to regard the promise as a brazen wall against every danger. In calling himself Abram's reward he teaches him to be satisfied with himself alone, and not simply a reward but an exceeding great reward, with which we ought to be more than sufficiently contented. Not that the faithful can be entirely free from fear while they are tossed by tempests, but the storm is hushed in their own breast, and faith triumphs over fear. Clarke asks whether Abram can have understood the words of temporal advantage; if he did, he was disappointed all his life, and the Israelites never enjoyed such affluence either. What then is intended is just what the words state: God was Abram's portion, and is the portion of every righteous soul. Wesley says it in a line — not only thy rewarder, but thy reward.
2:
Henry counts the complaint fourfold, and defends the act of complaining. Though we must never complain of God, we have leave to complain to him; it is some ease to a burdened spirit to open its case to a faithful and compassionate friend. Abram grieves that he had no child — not only no son, but no seed, the emphasis lying on the words to me; that he was never likely to have any, going down the hill apace; that his servants were likely to be to him instead of sons; and that the want of a son took away the comfort of all his enjoyments. Wesley presses the same emphasis on the word seed: if he had had a daughter, from her the promised Messiah might have come, who was to be the seed of the woman, but he had neither son nor daughter. Gill makes the complaint turn on that expectation. What signifies what thou givest me of temporal blessings, if thou withholdest the blessing of a child, from whom it might be hoped would spring the promised Messiah? All my wealth and riches, victories and honours are of no avail while I am deprived of this favour.

On whether the complaint was faulty they agree. Henry says that if we suppose Abram looked no further than a temporal comfort, it was culpable — it did ill become the father of the faithful to ask what wilt thou give me right after God had said, I am thy shield and thy exceeding great reward; but if he had an eye to the promised seed, the importunity of his desire was very commendable, since all was nothing to him while he was kept in the dark about the main matter. Yet thus far it was culpable, that there was some diffidence of the promise at the bottom of it, and a weariness of waiting God's time. Calvin grants that in overlooking a promise so glorious, and murmuring against God for having given him no seed, Abram seems to conduct himself with little modesty; but the liberty he took admits of excuse, first because the Lord permits us to pour into his bosom the cares by which we are tormented, and secondly because of its design. Seeing that the effect of all the promises depended upon his seed, he does not improperly require that a pledge so necessary should be given him; and this is why God not only regards the complaint with favour but immediately gives a propitious answer.

The name of the heir sets them arguing. Calvin reads the complaint as a runner's figure: our life is like a race, and Abram, of advanced age, has so far proceeded that little of his course remains, so that near the goal he shall die childless — and he adds, to aggravate the indignity, that a foreigner would be his heir. Calvin himself renders the rare Hebrew word as the son of the deserted house, since it was proof of a barren house that the inheritance devolved upon a foreigner who would occupy the empty place. Ellicott reports the usual explanation, the son of possession, that is the owner of the house when Abram dies, and another deriving the word from a verb meaning to run about, as if it were Eliezer's business to go to and fro on Abram's orders; but he thinks the rare term chosen chiefly for its play upon Dammesek, Damascus. On the phrase rendered one born in my house he is blunt: this is a mistake, for the Hebrew is the son of my house, not born of Abram but the chief of the household next to himself and its representative; Eliezer was probably born at Damascus. Clarke calls the Septuagint version at least curious, since it makes the rare word the name of a home-born maid whose son Eliezer was.
4:
Gill notes only that the word came again — either the vision had disappeared and came a second time, or God simply spoke to him once more. Calvin draws two inferences from the answer itself. First, that God had approved the wish of Abram; and from that follows the second, that Abram had not been impelled by any carnal affection to offer up this prayer, but by a pious and holy desire of enjoying the benediction promised to him. What is granted, moreover, exceeds what was asked: God not only promises him a seed, but a great people, who in number should equal the stars of heaven. Calvin will not turn this into allegory. Those who expound the passage of a heavenly seed which might be compared with the stars may enjoy their own opinion, but he maintains what he thinks more solid, that the faith of Abram was increased by the sight of the stars themselves.

Why a sign at all, Calvin explains from God's usual method: to affect his own people more deeply, and penetrate their minds more efficaciously, after he has reached their ears by his word he also arrests their eyes by external symbols, that eyes and ears may consent together. The sight was therefore not superfluous, but meant to strike Abram with this thought — he who by his word alone suddenly produced a host so numerous, by which he might adorn the previously vast and desolate heaven, shall he not be able to replenish my desolate house with offspring? Ellicott refuses to reduce the leading forth to a figure of speech. There is no reason for regarding it as a poetical description of a merely mental emotion: with his senses dormant, but alive to every spiritual impression, Abram feels himself led out from the tent into the open space around, and is there commanded to count. Gill leaves both readings open, saying it was done at God's call and direction, or by an impulse upon his mind, or else was not real and local at all, but only vision.

The hour is disputed. Clarke thinks the whole transaction took place in the evening, and that Abram had two visions, this one and the later sleep, the second bringing the revelation about the four hundred years. Wesley makes it early in the morning. Calvin holds that no nocturnal hour need be imagined at all, since the stars that escape our sight by day would then appear: the whole was transacted in vision, so that though Abram perhaps did not move a step, it was possible for him in vision to be led forth out of his tent. Ellicott observes that the stars visible to the naked eye are not in fact very numerous, but that they have ever been a received metaphor for an infinite multitude, probably because as men gaze they perpetually see the faint radiance of more and more distant constellations. Wesley reads the comparison for splendour as well as number: Abram's seed according to the flesh were like the dust of the earth, but his spiritual seed are like the stars of heaven. Calvin asks which seed is meant, and answers that the term is extended indiscriminately to the whole people God has adopted; but since many were alienated by unbelief, we must come for information to Christ, who alone distinguishes true and genuine sons from the illegitimate, and in whom the Gentiles also are by faith ingrafted into the body of Abram.
6:
Gill takes the object of Abram's trust as widely as the promise allows. The Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan read it as believing in the Word of the Lord, and Gill follows them: Abram credited the pledge of a seed, and a very numerous one; he held that the Messiah would spring from that seed; he rested on him as Saviour and Redeemer, and on his righteousness as justifying him before God. Wesley keeps rather to the temper of the believing. Abram took the truth of what God had now said, leaning upon the power and faithfulness of him who said it; and the apostle magnifies this and makes it a standing example — he was not weak, he staggered not at the promise, he was strong, he was fully persuaded. Wesley adds that it had lately struggled with unbelief in the complaint just made, and, coming off conqueror, was thus crowned and thus honoured. Clarke calls the verse one of the most important passages in the whole Old Testament, since it contains and specifies that doctrine of justification which engrosses so considerable a share of the epistles of Paul, and at the foundation of which lies the atonement made by the Son of God.

On the counting itself Clarke observes that there was no act in the case but that of the mind and heart, no labour of any kind; hence acquittal without merit, for here there could be none — nothing Abram did could purchase the salvation of the whole human race. It was the promise he credited, and in the blessedness of it he became a partaker. Ellicott calls the verse the germ of free justification, and rests his argument on where the narrator placed it: Abram was a holy man, who proved himself by his deeds, yet the reflection is inserted not after the offering of Isaac but in the account of this vision, where all he did was believe, and for that was accounted righteous. Calvin recovers the sense of the verb from its opposites. As those to whom iniquity is reckoned stand guilty at the bar, so those to whom uprightness is reckoned are approved as just; and therefore they trifle who apply the term to Abram's character as an honest man, as if it meant only that his neighbours held him blameless.

Calvin then presses the date. Abram was accounted just many years after his calling, after he had left his country a voluntary exile, after he had given himself to sanctity and had risen, by long exercise, to a life almost angelical. Many grant that the acquittal freely bestowed on the unworthy comes by believing alone, but restrict this to a moment, so that whoever begins so may afterwards be justified by good deeds, the one being merely the threshold and the other a continual course. Yet if the angelical uprightness of Abram, cultivated through so many years in one uniform course, did not keep him from fleeing hither for righteousness, where upon earth shall such perfection be found as may stand in God's sight? From the circumstance of time Calvin therefore gathers that holy men are justified so as long as they live in the world, and that what is related of one is applicable to all the sons of God. Wesley draws the same conclusion from another date: Abram was accepted while yet uncircumcised, and if he, so rich in good works, was not justified by them, much less can we be.
7:
Henry finds three encouragements packed into the one sentence. What God is in himself: I am Jehovah, and therefore I may give it thee, being sovereign Lord of all; I can give it thee, whatever opposition be made; and I will make good my word, for Jehovah is not a man that he should lie. What he had already done: he brought him out of Ur of the Chaldees, or, as some read it, out of the fire of the Chaldees, either from their idolatries, since the Chaldeans worshipped fire, or from their persecutions. Wesley repeats the Jewish tradition that Abram was cast into a fiery furnace and miraculously delivered, but judges with Henry that it is rather a place of that name; God brought him thence by an effectual call, snatching him as a brand out of the burning. And what God intended yet: not merely to possess the land, but to possess it as an inheritance, the sweetest and surest title. Calvin reads the same clause as a knot tied between two moments. God connects the promise he is about to give with the prior redemption — I do not now first begin to promise thee this land, for it was on this account that I brought thee out of thy own country.

The request for a sign is defended on all sides. Gill says it was not asked as questioning or doubting, but for the further confirmation of Abram's own persuasion, and for his posterity's sake, that they might the more strongly hold what was promised them; nor is it culpable to ask a sign with such a view, since Gideon and Hezekiah did so without blame, and Ahaz is blamed for refusing to ask one. Henry distinguishes it from the request of Zacharias: Abram believed already, and here prays rather against his own unbelief, desiring a token to be treasured up against an hour of temptation, not knowing by what event his confidence might yet be shaken and tried; and he desired it also for his descendants, since those satisfied themselves should wish others satisfied too. Ellicott makes the same point from the answer given: Abram asks not from want of trust but from a desire for more direct confirmation and fuller knowledge of the details, and what he receives is an exact and circumstantial prophecy in the form of a solemn covenant. Keil and Delitzsch put it shortest — the question was no expression of doubt, but of desire for the sealing of a promise which transcended human thought.

Calvin feels the objection more sharply than the rest and answers it at length. It may appear absurd that one who had rested on the bare word of God should now dispute whether what he hears from that mouth be true, and require an additional pledge. His answer is that the Lord sometimes concedes to his children that they may freely express any objection which comes into their mind, not acting so strictly as to refuse to be questioned. Indeed the more certainly Abram was persuaded that God was true, the more familiarly did he disburden his cares into God's bosom. The long delay was itself no small obstacle: after being held in suspense through a great part of his life, worn down with age and with nothing before his eyes but death and the grave, he now hears again that he shall be lord of the land. His questioning is therefore rather a proof than a sign of incredulity — though Calvin adds that there were special impulses in the saints of old which it would not now be lawful to draw into a precedent. Clarke lingers on the name Abram uses, which the Jews substitute for the ineffable one: it signifies director, basis, supporter, prop or stay, the buttress that shores up a building which otherwise must fall.
9:
Wesley notes what kind of token was given. Perhaps Abram expected something from heaven, but God gives him a sign upon a sacrifice; those who would receive the assurances of God's favour must attend instituted ordinances, and expect to meet him in them. Each beast was to be three years old, because then they were at their full growth and strength — God must be served with the best we have. Gill adds that these creatures were used in offering long before the ceremonial law was given, and marks the difference: the Levitical rule required animals of a year old, whereas these are at their fullest perfection. Clarke turns the list itself into an argument. Every animal allowed or commanded to be offered under the law of Moses is to be found here; and is this not a proof that God was giving Abram an epitome of that law, whose essence consisted in the sacrifices which typified the Lamb of God that takes away the sin of the world? He passes on Jarchi's reading: the idolatrous nations are likened in Scripture to bulls and rams and goats, and Israel to doves, so that the dividing of the carcases denotes the extermination of the nations, while the birds left whole show that Israel abides for ever.

The dividing is explained from the old rite of treaty-making. Clarke insists that an agreement supposes at least two parties, since one cannot be made between an individual and himself; and that for whatever purpose it was struck, it was ever ratified by a victim offered to God, the parties then walking between the severed halves. That walking signified that each agreed, if he broke his engagement, to submit to the punishment of being cut asunder — a mode of execution Clarke documents from Herodotus, from Daniel, and from the imprecation Livy preserves, in which the Roman priest, killing a hog, prayed that Jupiter would so smite his own people if they first transgressed. Calvin gives the rite a gentler turn: the allies or the soldiers passed between the parts so that, being enclosed together within the victim, they might be the more sacredly united in one body; and Jeremiah bears witness that the practice was known among the Jews, where princes and nobles and the whole people passed between the divisions of the calf. Clarke accounts for the one exception by the later statute — the birds he divided not, since under the law fowls were not to be cut asunder but only cloven for the taking out of the intestines.

Calvin refuses to allegorise every part, saying that certain interpreters weary themselves in the fabrication of subtleties whereas our business is to cultivate sobriety; he confesses he does not know why three kinds of beast were named besides the birds. The sum, in his judgment, is that God, in commanding the animals to be killed, shows what the future condition of the Church will be. Abram wished to be assured of the promised inheritance, and is taught that it would take its commencement from death — he and his children must die before they enjoy the land; and the servitude with which they were oppressed was more intolerable than simple death, yet because the offering is made to God, death itself is immediately turned into new life. That is why Abram, laying the parts opposite each other, fits them one to the other: they were again to be gathered from their dispersion. Gill reads the birds of prey as the Egyptians and the other enemies of Israel, citing the Targum of Jonathan, that the idolatrous nations descended, like an unclean fowl, to spoil the goods of the Israelites. Ellicott observes that a fire would have kept the vultures off, but the bodies lay exposed, so Abram kept guard lest the ceremonial be frustrated.
12:
Henry sets the hour against the whole day's waiting. The orders about the victims had come early, while the stars were still to be seen, and preparing them was Abram's morning work; then he abode by the pieces, praying and watching until towards evening, about the time of the evening oblation. God often keeps his people long in expectation of the comforts he designs them; the answers of prayer come slowly, but surely. Wesley distinguishes the sleep that then fell on him from any other: not a common sleep through weariness or carelessness, but a divine ecstasy, so that, taken off from things sensible, he might be wholly taken up with the contemplation of things spiritual — the doors of the body locked up, that the soul might be private and act the more freely. Clarke notes that the word is the same used of the trance into which Adam was cast before the woman was formed, and that the horror of great darkness was designed to express the affliction and misery into which the posterity of Abram should be brought during their bondage. Gill lingers on the hour itself: the sun just setting, about to enter into his chamber, whence he went forth in the morning as a strong man to run his race.

On what the darkness meant, four readings converge. Henry marks the suddenness of the change — just before, Abram was solacing himself in the comforts of God's covenant, and now this falls on him; the children of light do not always walk in the light. He gives it three uses: to strike an awe upon Abram, that the familiarity God allowed him might not breed contempt, since holy fear prepares the soul for holy joy; to be a specimen of God's dealings with his seed, who must first know the gloom of Egyptian slavery before entering the good land with joy; and to indicate the nature of the older dispensation, one of obscurity and of dread. Keil and Delitzsch read the hour symbolically: the setting of the sun prefigured the departure of the sun of grace which shone upon Israel, and the beginning of a dark and dreadful period of suffering, the very anticipation of which involved Abram in darkness. Ellicott holds the terror was not mental so much as bodily, caused by a deep gloom settling round him, such as would follow an eclipse of the setting sun and shut all mortal things away from his view. Calvin says the vision is now mingled with a dream, the horror intervening that Abram might know it was no common dream but divinely conducted.

The oracle that follows is all hardship, and Calvin thinks the order deliberate. Before one son is given him, Abram hears that his seed shall be long in captivity and slavery; for thus the Lord deals with his own, always making a beginning from death, so that by quickening the dead he may the more abundantly show his power. Three things are brought forward step by step: that the sons of Abram must wander before they attain the promised inheritance, that they should be slaves, and that they were to be inhumanly and tyrannically treated. Wherefore his faith was admirable and singular, since he acquiesced in an oracle so sorrowful. Henry parcels out the same three: they shall be strangers, first in Canaan and then in Egypt, for before they were lords of their own land they were strangers in a strange one; they shall be servants, and what was the doom of the Canaanites becomes the distress of Abram's seed, with this difference, that the one serve under a curse and the other under a blessing; and they shall be sufferers, since those whom God loves are often sorely afflicted by wicked men. Wesley traces the course of that affliction from mocking to the murder of the new-born.
14:
Gill notes the precision of the word: it is not said the land in which they were strangers, but the nation they should serve, meaning the Egyptians, whom the Lord threatens to enter into judgment with and take vengeance upon, as he did by the ten plagues. Wesley makes the same identification and draws the rule from it: the punishing of persecutors is the judging of them, a righteous thing with God, and a particular act of justice to recompense tribulation to those that trouble his people. Clarke measures the promise by its fulfilment — in the redemption of Israel from bondage, in the plagues and destruction of the Egyptians, and in the immense wealth the Israelites brought out with them, not a more circumstantial or literally fulfilled promise is to be found in the sacred writings. Ellicott explains why the country is left unnamed. Had it been expressly revealed that Egypt would afflict them, the patriarchs might have been unwilling to go thither; but the reference to the judgment and to the great substance gave detail enough for future guidance, and assurance afterwards that the word had been kept.

Calvin takes the sentence as a consolation, of which the first part is that God testifies he will be the vindicator of his people; whence it follows that he takes upon himself the care of the salvation of those he has embraced, and will not suffer them to be harassed by the wicked with impunity. Though vengeance is here announced upon Egypt only, all the enemies of the Church lie under the same judgment, as Moses in his song extends to every age the threat that the Lord will punish unjust persecutions. Whenever tyrants treat us with inhumanity, which is very usual with the Church, let this be our consolation: that after our trust has been sufficiently proved by bearing the cross, God, at whose pleasure we are thus humbled, will himself be the Judge, and will repay our enemies the due reward of the cruelty they now exercise. Though they exult with intoxicated joy, it will at length appear by the event itself that our miseries are happy ones and their triumphs wretched. But we must give place unto the wrath of God, Calvin adds with Paul, that we may not be hurried headlong to seek revenge; and place must be given to hope also, that it may sustain us when we are oppressed and groaning under the burden of evils.

The promise made to Abram himself turns on two words. Gill hears in going to the fathers a passage out of this world to another, to the world of spirits, and calls it no inconsiderable proof of the immortality of the soul; and in going in peace, a release from all the fatigues of his pilgrimage, a sparing him the sight of his posterity's afflictions, and tranquillity of mind in one who knew in whom he had believed. Clarke reads the same two things distinctly marked: the soul of Abram introduced among the assembly of the first-born, and the body buried after a long life. Ellicott observes that Abram's ancestors had died in Babylonia, so that the body may be buried far away while the soul joins the company of its forefathers in some separate abode, not to be absorbed but still to enjoy a personal existence. Calvin dismisses as frigid the gloss that only a natural and painless death is meant; what is promised is a placid old age with a joyful death answering to it, and since men have no such close of life in their own power, the Lord teaches by promising it that it is his own gift. Wesley adds the marks of an old age worth calling good: old and healthful, old and holy, old and useful, old and exemplary for godliness.
16:
The counting of the generations is not settled. Gill takes it of the descendants of those who went down into Egypt — Moses and Aaron being fourth from Levi, and Caleb fourth from Judah — or rather of the fourth age reckoned from the birth of Isaac, men then living about a hundred years apiece; and he notes that Grotius applied it instead to the Amorites, because of the clause that follows. Clarke observes that in former times most peoples counted by generations, and that the term assigned to each varied widely from nation to nation and age to age, so that it is probable the phrase here means the same span as the figure given in the preceding sentence; he reports the rival views, that it points to Eleazar dividing the land, or again to the Amorites. Ellicott, taking generation and century as equivalents here, finds an undesigned testimony to the long duration of human life then: Abram was a hundred years old at the birth of Isaac, and Isaac sixty at the birth of his sons. He adds that the Hebrew word had probably come down from a remote antiquity and, like the Latin seculum, signified an age.

The reason for the delay is stated as a moral one. Wesley puts it plainly: the seed of Abram must be kept out of possession because the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full, the righteous God having determined that they should not be cut off until they had arrived at such a pitch of wickedness. Clarke draws the general rule out of it — there is a certain pitch of iniquity to which nations may arrive before they are destroyed, and beyond which divine justice does not permit them to pass. Ellicott takes the Amorites, as the chief and leading tribe, to stand for all the Canaanite nations, and makes the clause govern the whole conquest: they were not extirpated by any wilful decree to make room for Israel, but as an act of justice, like that which for their moral depravity overwhelmed the men before the flood. So it has been throughout history: wherever nations settle down in vice and corruption, the decay of their institutions follows that of their morals, and they either waste away or give place to some more manly race of conquerors. The conquest of Canaan was parallel to that of the enervated Roman empire of the West by the Germans; only here we see the preparation for it, and the purpose of God explained.

Calvin meets the objection that this makes the salvation of Abram's sons depend on the destruction of others. We must with modesty and humility yield to the secret counsel of God. Since he had given that land to the Amorites to be inhabited by them, he intimates that he will not without just cause transfer the possession of it: I grant the dominion of this land to thy seed without injury to any one, for it is occupied by its lawful possessors, to whom I delivered it, and until they have deserved by their sins to be rightfully expelled, it will not come to thy posterity. The passage is remarkable, Calvin says, as showing that the abodes of men are so distributed in the world that the Lord will preserve quiet people, each in their several stations, till they cast themselves out by their own wickedness; He also finds a commendation of the divine longsuffering: the Amorites had already become unworthy of the land, yet God bore with them and granted them long space for repentance. But the more graciously he waits, the more severely he avenges obstinacy at the last — as a heathen writer said, the anger of God proceeds with a slow step, but compensates for its tardiness by the severity of its punishment.
17:
Gill marks the hour: the sun was going down when the deep sleep fell, and now it was quite set. Henry reads the two objects as a single message in two halves. The smoking furnace signified the affliction of his seed in Egypt, where they were in the iron furnace, labouring in the very fire, and in the smoke, their eyes darkened so that they could not see the end of their troubles. The burning lamp denotes comfort in that affliction, and God showed it at the same moment: light for deliverance out of the furnace, a lamp for direction in the smoke, since God's word was their lamp in a dark place and perhaps prefigured the pillar of cloud and fire; and a burning lamp also for the destruction of the enemies who kept them there, since the same cloud that enlightened Israel troubled and burned the Egyptians. Clarke agrees about the furnace but is firmer about the flame: the burning lamp was certainly the symbol of the divine presence, which, passing between the pieces, ratified the covenant. Ellicott identifies the vessel as the circular firepot Orientals set in their houses to sit round for warmth, wreathed here in smoke, out of which shot a torch of flame — for not two symbols but one passed between the carcases.

Calvin makes the two appearances answer each other. At first Abram was horror-struck with the thick darkness; now, in the midst of a smoking furnace, he sees a burning lamp. Many suppose the fire consumed the sacrifice, but Calvin rather takes it as a symbol of future deliverance, since the obscurity of smoke and the shining of a lamp are contrary in appearance, and Abram thus learned that light would at length emerge out of darkness. The condition of the Church could not be painted more to the life than when God causes a burning torch to proceed out of the smoke, so that the darkness of afflictions may not overwhelm us, but we may cherish a good hope of life even in death. Keil and Delitzsch explain the transaction from the noun itself, which comes from a root meaning to cut, and denotes literally the bond concluded by cutting up the sacrificial animals. Clarke says the same of the verb, to cut a covenant, since none was ever made without a victim; the Romans likewise spoke of smiting or cleaving an agreement. Henry thinks it probable that the furnace and lamp burnt and consumed the pieces, so completing the offering and testifying God's acceptance of it, as fire did for Gideon and for Manoah and for Solomon.

Wesley notices that the tense of the grant has changed. God had said before, to thy seed will I give this land, and here says, I have given it: the charter is sealed and delivered and cannot be disannulled, and the possession is as sure in due time as if now made over to them. The present occupants are named so that their number and strength and long prescription should be no hindrance to the promise in its season. The southern boundary divides the commentators. Keil and Delitzsch take the two great rivers as the limits within which the seed of Abram would hold the land, and insist that the word here means the Nile, not the brook of Egypt, the boundary stream of the wilderness. Ellicott agrees, observing that the Hebrew always distinguishes the winter torrent of the southern border from the river that flows constantly, though our version neglects the distinction; so Abram's posterity are to found a kingdom conterminous with Egypt and Babylonia, bounds large and vague until the ten named nations limit them. Clarke dissents, taking it for the stream near the isthmus of Suez rather than the Nile, and holds that the promise was fully accomplished under David and Solomon.
19:
The list is longer here than it is later, and both commentators notice it. Gill reckons ten nations as occupying the land of Canaan at this time, whereas only seven are named in the days of Moses and Joshua; the three that are wanting seem before those times to have become extinct, or to have been mixed with the others and so no longer distinct. He records the alternatives: Aben Ezra thinks the same peoples went under two names, while Jarchi, following the Jerusalem Talmud, interprets the three of the Edomites, Moabites and Ammonites, who were to fall to the children of Israel in later times. Clarke reaches the same conclusion more briefly, judging it probable that some of the nations existing in Abram's day had been blended with others before the age of Moses, so that seven only of the ten then remained.

On the three vanished peoples Ellicott is fullest. The Kenites he calls an Arab race, found both among the Amalekites in the south and among the tribes of Naphtali and Zebulon in the north, and even in Midian, since Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, is called a Kenite; Balaam speaks of them as a powerful nation, and their wide dispersion into feeble remnants seems to show that they were early settlers in Canaan who, like the Rephaim, had been overpowered and scattered by later immigrants. They were uniformly friendly to Israel. Of the Kenizzites the chief fact of importance is that Caleb was one, who apparently with his clan joined the Israelites at the Exodus and was numbered with the tribe of Judah. The Kadmonites may mean either an eastern or an ancient people, of whom we know nothing. Gill traces the Kenites the same way to Jethro and to Heber, and notes their neighbourhood to the Amalekites in the days of Balaam and of Saul, and the house of Rechab that descended from them. Of the rest he says only where they lived: the Hittites, named from a son of Canaan, about Hebron in the south; the Amorites on both sides of Jordan; and the Jebusites in Jerusalem and about it, which was first called Jebus from the founder of that nation.

Clarke closes the chapter with three things he thinks must interest the pious reader. The first is the condescension of God in revealing himself to mankind in a variety of ways, so unequivocal that on the minds of those to whom the discoveries were made not one doubt was left, either of the truth of the subject or that God himself had spoken; and the subject of the discovery attested its own truth to all future generations, since it concerned matters then in futurity, so distinctly marked and so positively promised as to remain objects of attention and desire till they came. The second is the way of salvation, which now began to be explicitly declared: God gives the promise by means in which it was, humanly speaking, impossible that it should take place, teaching that the whole work was spiritual and divine, and that no human power could suffice to produce it. The third is that the foundation of the doctrine is laid in the covenant made between God and Abram on behalf of all the families of the earth, and that this covenant is ratified by a sacrifice; and since it still stands open, every human soul must ratify it for itself.
